text: This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. • Critical components such as large power transformers (essential for efficiently delivering power over long distances, converting voltage levels, and ensuring reliable and safe grid operation) are in short supply in the United States, leaving the grid vulnerable when transformers are damaged by intentional attacks or environmental factors. Many transformers, particularly distribution transformers, have already exceeded their design life expectancy (McKenna et al. 2024). Transformer supply lead times, especially those of large power transformers, have nearly tripled in the past several years, increasing from 50 weeks in 2021 to an average of 120 weeks in 2024 (Chopra and Boucher 2024). Further, the United States is heavily reliant on foreign-manufactured large power transformers, with more than 80% of demand being met by imports (DOE EERE 2022). • Increasing electricity demand, driven by factors such as the proliferation of data centers, is straining the grid’s capacity. Data center load growth has tripled in the past decade and is projected to again double or triple by 2028, potentially overtaking DOW electricity demand and diminishing DOW’s influence on grid requirements (Shehabi et al. 2024). • Studies project that intraregional transmission needs will increase 20% by 2035 to accommodate moderate load growth and more with high load growth. Current plans might not ensure enough generation and transmission infrastructure to meet demand (DOE 2023). Regulatory challenges, environmental concerns, and local opposition have hindered transmission build-out that would support load growth (McLaughlin 2025). Moreover, U.S. grid operators cite complexity and a lack of software vendors as impediments to upgrading transmission lines and carrying capacity, potentially delaying improvements by years (McLaughlin 2025). Dependence on local utility grids accentuates a vulnerability associated with nonuniformity across utilities in critical mission prioritization, in part because countries, states, and localities have distinct energy policies, regulatory frameworks, and market dynamics that influence how power providers allocate resources. For example, states with more aggressive advanced energy adoption mandates may focus more on transitioning away from legacy energy sources, whereas others might prioritize traditional power generation methods to support critical infrastructure (REN21 2023). Additionally, most advanced economies’ utility distribution systems (including in the United States) use aging infrastructure that will require significant improvement for larger energy demands (IEA 2023). The reserve capacity for potential military surge needs could differ across utilities and regions as well. This patchwork of policies and priorities can lead to inconsistencies in how critical missions are supported across different regions, impeding DOW’s ability to anticipate risks and ensure energy resilience. Moreover, in the United States, some distribution providers and cooperatives are not required to follow Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards for cybersecurity, so cybersecurity investments compete against other investments that support reliability, enhance performance, or lower consumer rates. Partnering with local utilities at home and abroad could help clarify these entities’ challenges and improve cybersecurity.
